title: Nobody Taught the Teachers
author: The Walled Garden
summary: The fourth installment of a six-part series on 'Attentional Literacy' argues that teacher training programs never actually teach teachers the science of attention, despite professional standards in Ontario, British Columbia, England, and Australia all explicitly requiring teachers to know current research on how students learn. The author contrasts this with a rugby coaching session that transformed their soccer coaching practice through evidence-backed, explainable methods, noting coaching gets a built-in feedback loop (a scoreline) that teaching lacks. Citing doctoral researcher Rachel Moylan's finding that most teacher digital-competence frameworks require no knowledge of algorithms, the author argues attentional literacy suffers the identical blind spot, and blames a teacher-training pipeline that has previously let unvetted theories like Learning Styles and Whole-Language Reading Instruction take root uncontested. The piece's key structural argument is that attention is a shared resource that flows between classrooms all day, meaning individual teacher autonomy cannot substitute for a common, well-informed standard.
points: The professional-standards argument is the piece's backbone: teacher licensing standards in Ontario, British Columbia, England, and Australia all explicitly require teachers to know current research on student learning, yet attentional science is absent from training pipelines.

Doctoral researcher Rachel Moylan's audit found that most frameworks defining teachers' 'professional digital competence' require no knowledge of algorithms at all, which the author argues is the same blind spot afflicting attentional literacy.

The coaching-versus-teaching contrast is sharp: a match ends with a score, giving coaches a built-in feedback loop, while classroom outcomes are murkier, making it easier for unvalidated practices to go unchallenged for years.

The piece's structural argument against relying on teacher autonomy: attention is 'a shared resource that numerous adults draw on and deposit into throughout the school day,' so one teacher's habits directly affect what the next teacher inherits.
quotes: We don't need more techniques for manufacturing engagement; we need better information about how our students' minds work.
It's a teacher's job description to know the research bearing on how children learn, and to keep knowing how it changes. That is a condition of their licence.
It concludes that we retain what we retrieve better than what we review, that material spaced across weeks or months is easier to remember than what we cram into a single session.
She found that most require no knowledge of algorithms at all, despite their ubiquitous presence in our lives.
Unfounded and debunked theories like Learning Styles and Whole-Language Reading Instruction found purchase within training programmes themselves, and affected whole generations of students.
That is not a failure of teachers. It is a failure to teach them.
